commentBody:
"By Kevin Curry and Zhou Zhang"

Squeal!!!!

I foresee a hip, hip, hurumba in my near future!
I frantically scrambled to get to the end of this puzzle, but after I finished and took a step back, I realize that this is a really clever construction! Thanks Kevin and Zhou!

Spectacular! Sunday POY nominee. Perfect for solving on the stone tablet delivered to my cave. Seeing the entire puzzle all the time was a joy, and it was very helpful for maze travel. I definitely BE AMAZED.
I really enjoyed this one.  Didn’t see the end coming!

For me, a defining moment of my friendship with Zhou came after I test-solved this puzzle. She asked me how I'd prefer the beginning and ending theme squares to be represented—rebuses or maybe images—and I texted "Images. I hate rebuses!" Despite learning that she and Kevin love rebuses, Zhou is so amazing that I still wanted to be friends. As a proud member of Team Zhou who still scowls a little at rebuses, it's a nice compromise to see the rebuses turn into images. Three cheers for Zhou and Kevin!
Somehow I got a new personal best time on this one, but it didn’t feel inordinately easy. Pretty cute. ◡̈

"How's the cheese?"
"Not the best. But it's gouda-nough."

("What grade would you give it?"
"Brie plus.")

Delightful! Before retiring, I taught psychology, so it was amusing to figure out the answer to 1a about halfway through, which helped me fill in the shaded squares quickly, and then, after nearly completing the puzzle, to travel the maze to figure out the meaning of the circled letters. I usually work from bottom to top, so I got the rebus quite early; sorry for stealing your cheese, my furry friend!
A wonderful, enjoyable puzzle, thank you!

Thank you for a delightful puzzle!  I needed no cheats, but had two typos that took awhile to find.

More like this one, please!
Ok, I give … what’s the name of the book? HWOVEOMDOMM. I know I’m missing something, and will feel sheepish when it’s pointed out to me!,

Maybe it's just me, but I found it impossible to determine the path.  I was able to complete the grid and see the book title, but the instruction to "travel the maze" made me think a maze would be apparent and visible.  It was not.

This was so fun!! And I did it almost all by myself!

Today I filled in heaps just from my own knowledge, plus some Googling but actually I think less than usual. Then I had the grid full and I’d worked out the LABRAT situation, but something was still wrong… it was time to turn to the article, where I discovered that I had missed the rebus (can’t believe I didn’t spot that one myself - I knew something was off down there!) and then, ta-da! I did it. 🤩

Definitely starting to improve at this crossword thing.

ILIKE, ILIKE!  What else could these two incredible constructors do but AMAZE us!? They really are a big dill, in my book! (Favorite clue, by the way.) Enjoyed the animations at the end too! Just terrific!! 

Went a bit too fast, though I made one truly bone-headed mistake. At 74A, I was confidently thinking of wine country, which I know is NAPA, but for some reason, instead I wrote NAsA....  D'oh! I just moved on and since I didn't know the guitar risers. Gave myself a good Captain Picard facepalm when I realized what I did. 

Of course, I'd always prefer LEVAR clued to Star Trek, but I'm a big LEVAR fan too and love all he does for literacy, so all good! 

And IDRIS, who was in a Star Trek (well, one of the sort of rebooted ones) and in THOR is also pretty great! 

Kevin and Zhou, please give us MAS MORE!  And thank you! You bring UTTER delight! 

Hip, hip, hurrumba!!
A-MAZE-ing!!
I LOVED this one. So many fun things all rolled into one.
Loved this puzzle, and especially the cleverness of the shaded squares—truly, I was a-maze-d!

Pretty mellow solve, except I messed myself in the upper left corner because I confidently plunked Romano in where ASIAGO belonged. Once that was fixed, I got the rest of the corner, including our LAB RAT.  
I'm not a big fan of trying to solve things with letters in circles scattered throughout the puzzle, but lucky for me the puzzle drew the maze by itself almost as soon as I was finished. I expect this may be a bug rather than a feature for some.

Wonderfully twisty puzzle from my favorite constructors who certainly didn’t disappoint today, I’m glad you stuck with it! Definitely on my POY list.

Clever idea, terrific construction, multiple layers, and great accessory fill and clues. Don’t know if it was deliberate or a gift from the crossword gods but DONTINTERRUPTME was a great side note.

For crossword construction geeks, notice that the grid was almost but not quite symmetrical (the middle is a bit random). I assume this was necessary for better fill or to make the construction work, but it’s a great misdirection for a maze as well. 

By the way the book referenced is a great short self-help book and an excellent primer on both business and life, and still worth the read.

No particular clues to comment on today except anyone else think about targeting ABS (with specific exercises) before ADS?

Thanks again, Zhou and Kevin for providing a great Halloween maze to solve!
Good Sunday puzzle

That was a fun solve. I would have been perfectly happy if the maze solution had been left for solvers to discover, instead of being broadcast by some tech trick. This way, the maze has had no connection with my solve.
It was definitely fun, though I solved it much faster than average. Also, I would've like a chance to do the maze! Still cool though

I picked up on the shaded square commonality rather quickly, but didn't grasp the full theme as I neglected to look at the puzzle title until I was already done (a rookie Sunday mistake!)

My own blundering aside, what a fun solve! I'm no Algernon, but I was on the right wavelength today and enjoyed this tremendously

That was a twisty journey! Because I print it out, I had no cues about the direction of the maze or solving the 1998 title via the circled letters. Going left to right or up and down didn't work. I was lost for quite a while, looking at the 10 letters and creating various possible anagrams...at one point I had HOW and DOOM but the remaining letters didn't form a word. I saw MOODY and HOW MY MODE...

I even got as far as WHO MOVED but somehow hallucinated an extra D, so I couldn't figure out WHO MOVED DYM, lol! So I came here and Caitlin's initial cues helped and suddenly, OH, I got out my red pencil and followed the maze, avoiding the gray obstacles (so clever!) and black squares. Tada! Very satisfying and fun. Thanks, Zhou and Kevin. Now I printed out Patrick's 2005 maze puzzle and, since we get an extra hour tonight, I'll tackle that next.
OK that was cool.

Oh, well, putting this grid together to make it work is impressive enough, actually an astounding achievement for Kevin and Zhou. The fact that they made 30 grids that they weren’t satisfied with, AND KEPT ON to the 31st, the one that passed their bar, shows they have the work ethic to make the astounding happen.

It also shows that their prime motivation is excellence rather than “see what I can do?”.

And look what they did from the seed idea of having white squares in a puzzle act like black squares – made a maze where non-black squares are barrier walls.  Then add the level of the book title, related to the theme, where the circled letters help the solver figure out the route.  

Imagination, wit, inspiring perseverance, leading to utter vibrancy in the box today.

Well, for me, the backstory is amazing.  As amazing as this puzzle was fun to fill in.  Thank you, Kevin and Zhou for all you put into this, and for a most splendid outing today!
One of my fastest Sunday solves, but didn't get the theme until coming here and reading about it. Clever. Just apparently too clever for me!
Relaxing solve, what a great puzzle

A quick bit of fun this evening! I'm glad they stuck with the concept, and I'm almost sorry that it didn't take me longer to finish. Made a few wrong guesses along the way, but they were corrected quickly.

Thanks, Zhou and Kevin!

Been playing too much Crossplay. Had sweep before BINGO! Watched Game 7 while playing and still came in well under average time.

Now nothing left to do but hit the gym and early vote tomorrow.
I never comment but I absolutely loved this puzzle, and reading about their history was ADORBS! I loved their escape room puzzle last year, too. What a great pair of constructors. Bravo!
longtime solver, first time commenter, but just have to say I’m in awe of this construction. what a fun one!
To my great embarrassment, for the longest time I had LABBAT in place of LABRAT. You can take the Canadian out of Canada, but...etc.
A quick puzzle, but cute!
There were shaded squares but did not see circles online on phone. Solved without getting any of the subtleties except all the shaded words were similar. Can someone explain to me? Thanks!

This past week I made an embarrassing mistake in the comments. While praising a puzzle by Katie Hoody, I got her mixed up with Zhou Zhang. (Don’t ask. Lewis set me straight. Sorry, Katie & Zhou!) I’m a big fan of both constructors (and Kevin Curry) so it was great to see Zhou and Kevin’s great puzzle today so soon after my faux pas, as if to make sure I know who’s who. (I do.) And Friday was brought to us by Robyn Weintraub and Rafael Musa. What a line-up these past few days! Thank you all!

I had a lot of fun with this puzzle and I liked the cluing in general.

The single square rebus though, no, that's terrible.  I like rebus puzzles but when they make most of the puzzle normal and put it in one single square it feels like a contract violation, the same way that puzzle where you needed six hyphens did.  Thursday and Sunday are all about rule changes but keep it within the shared understanding of which rules get changed.  Don't randomly put punctuation in the puzzle, don't make one single square a rebus and nothing else.

Other than that great puzzle.
Swing and a miss
Flabbergasting constructing chops totally trumped utterly underwhelming theme for me.

Wonderful.

I feel like I should say more.

Really wonderful.
Stuck for what felt like an eternity in the northwest corner because I have MOghol instead of MONGOL. It finally clicked after an eon. Phew.

This is the best one since the Mario one earlier this year. That final clue was the perfect “AHA!”… until I realised I screwed up the middle clue and had to look up the answer because STONEWALL didn’t seem like a valid answer for a slingshot. Oh well, that’s on me. Bravo!
What a fun idea and excellent execution! I had a great time from RAT to CHEESE!

Fun puzzle and theme!  Glad I remembered to look at the info page and I saw the Note. I had a moment wondering who Labrat was, then I recognized the dook.  I looked in the bottom corner for the goal and I said cheese fairly early in my solve.  The memorable book title came to me.  Then I worked various areas in a  random order to finish. After the first obstacle course I enjoyed filling in the bumpers.  A Sunday puzzle of the year contender.
I am, in a word, AWESTRUCK!  Best puzzle ever!
Really fun.
This was such a fun puzzle! Perfect Sunday crossword. A maze within a crossword … 👌👌

How many puzzles did we get today? Let’s see:
1. Five clues containing words that are mysteriously connected.
2. Eleven squares that spell out a phrase.
3. One of them is a rebus!
4. And all of it ties together with a maze.

Puzzles within puzzles, my absolute favorite. And this was among the best. 💐 Can Zhou and Kevin do all the Sunday puzzles? And maybe all the Thursdays, too?
That was absolutely fun!  And very clever!
Absolutely LOVED this. How clever and so much fun to do!

Decent puzzle overall. I find puzzles with a single rebus slightly annoying, but not that big a deal. However: 
43D: Giving permission does not necessarily enable. You can give me permission to dunk on Michael Jordan, but it's not gonna happen. This also came up in the December 28, 2022 puzzle; interestingly, it was 42D in that puzzle. 
45A: If the answer is a comparative (or superlative), the clue should match.
first time i’ve solved a Sunday crossword on my own in one go and without any help 😊

🏋️🚪

(Rebus DumbellDoor)
Very clever. Not hints or Google needed. I questioned a couple of clues, but no big deal. Fun solve. Thank you.

Cute puzzle. No real challenges, but I enjoyed a nice, quick solve after toiling a bit the last two days.

First time in a while I haven't had to rehash the grid to find a typo or two, so duly satisfied today! 

I suppose whether you loved or hated this one depends on your mood.

Always, but especially today, I'm so glad I solve on paper!  

Once again, Zhou and Kevin cooked up something that not only shows off their talent as constructors, but their attention to the details that make for a fun solve.  Great job!
Oh I see it "Who moved my cheese!🧀". Love mazes and loved this puzzle. Enjoyed reading about the creative process. Thanks Zhou and Kevin.

I solved the NW corner first so I could get a clue as to the theme.  As I made my way through the puzzle, I didn’t see anything that seemed related to LABRATs, and the darkened and circled squares didn’t make any sense to me.  By the time I got to the CHEESE rebus, I’d forgotten all about the LABRAT from 1A.  I briefly checked if any of the other circled squares were rebuses, saw that they weren’t,  and shrugged.  When I plugged in my final letter I got a true aha moment when the delightful graphic flashed on.  Well done Zhou and Kevin: a charming Sunday puzzle with a cute graphic reward at the end of the maze.

Completely tickled by this one -- this has to be an all-timer! I'm especially amused because I have a friend who recently made an art series based on the book featured here -- and, at the remove of decades, guys, that book is so gloriously absurd, with a central fable about a pair of mice (Sniff and Scurry) and a pair of mouse-sized people (Hem and Haw) commuting to a maze, having their cheese unjustly moved, and being encouraged via business proverbs to unthinking acceptance of the situation. It's like if a TED talk came to life and tried to write Watership Down. Anyway, awesome crossword.
The maze contributed absolutely nothing to this puzzle. I solved it without any consideration of it. I understood there were "Barrier"s and "Wall"s but I just ignored them.

I think I messed up the solving on this one. I liked the lab rat getting its rebus cheese, and noticing the themed entries helped fill in a lot of the grid. However, it seemed to fill in so quickly (and very unusually without any lookups for me today) that there wasn't time to do anything with the maze or circled letters before it was all done for me at the end. This one clearly lends itself to being solved on paper... Having said that, I've never heard of the book, so I don't know how satisfying it would've been to go through it all.
Petition for more rebuses in puzzles, I really love them and this one only teased me with its lone (but fun!) entry!

Well done all around, a big round of applause for the constructors and editors!

Sunday puzzles are usually my least favorite, but this one solved like a midweek themeless that kept me interested.

I had been stumped by the NW the first time through so when I ended up back there to finish there was a nice payoff.  I'm sure that was by design.
What a hoot! Wicked fun puzzle—wonderfully designed and clued.

Since there seems to be a strong divide between the lovers and the meh-to-haters today, I am voting with the “good construct, fun solve crowd”, since every vote matters!  

For the US solvers, don’t forget to vote by Tuesday either!
Fabulous! I love interlocking theme elements and using the grid visually as a component of the puzzle. This had both! And fun (if a bit easy) to solve. Contender for POY for sure.

Wow. I totes ADORBs this. Yes, a little easier for a Sunday, but the payoff was the fun of working out the game, following the trail and landing on the rebus. I don’t know the book but finding the title only added to the fun.

Thank you for this reasonably gentle grid, I’m a tad delicate after last night’s Halloween disco. The witches brew cocktail went down very well. There are a few sore heads in the village this morning, including one chap who curled up and went to sleep in the corner after consuming vast quantities of said brew. This despite the speakers blasting music a few feet from his head. BLESS.

FOR ALL GAUCHOS, NEAR AND FAR: 

41-ACROSS is for us. 

They can never take it away from us. 

For one day, all around the globe, humanity (re: crossword-ers) had to puzzle through a four-letter Spanish word that took us all back to Del Playa (on the day after Halloween, no less!)...Storke Tower...and four (or five, or five-plus) of the best years of our young lives. 

Go UCSB. Go Gauchos. 

Go...us.
A fabulous trip!  However, I was hung up until the end in the NW corner, because the “Alternative to Parmesan” is obviously ROMANO…  :)
Other than not wanting to be reminded of DOGE anything, I enjoyed this puzzle today.

Solved without hints, not uncommon for a Sunday I suppose, but I surprised myself as many of the answers were unknown to me.  I stall don't know what the circled letters say, but that didn't stop me from enjoying the post-game animation.

I haven't read the comments yet and fear that some will find the puzzle too cute, but I thought it was a good Sunday morning romp.

Looks like this was a favourite. I solved most of the clues, (not CAT CONDO - cats have furniture? and DOGE COIN, LEVAR or the songs) and at the end the red lines appeared.

I can see it's clever but I don't see how it relates to doing a crossword. I would have preferred better clues. I liked EARS, that was funny, SLUICE and OLD TALES were tricky adjacent,  but the rest -  a lot of synonyms and general knowledge. Legs on a butterfly. EROICA. Just not my favourite.
This is so clever, brightened my day.

Much appreciated the clever, painstaking grid construction. Even without the circled book-title letters, there really is only one broad path that the LABRAT can follow to the end without hitting black squares or a gray wall, barrier, etc. 

Given the maze concept with its constraints on the LABRAT's movement, I enjoyed seeing SLUICE featured, given that a SLUICE and its gates help regulate when and how much water can move from place to place. (And glad to have read Graham Swift’s Waterland, in which a SLUICE plays a prominent role, so happily, that entry flowed in smoothly!) 

Overall, quite a gentle puzzle with a nice reward, so no need to call PETA. Thanks, Kevin Curry and Zhou Zhang! Glad you persisted through your own crafting and publication maze.
I’m not too proud to admit I needed this one today, after Saturday’s grid stopped me like a brick WALL.

Klunky.  Perhaps a lack of vision on my part, but even after reading the painfully precise instructions in the column, the path the critter takes still seems mostly arbitrary to me.  I didn't mind the single rebus, but the whole thing felt off and middling to me.  Sad because I recall always liking Zhang's work (though not so much her partner's).  And yes of course I read the circles.  Oh well.
I read that book at a low point in my carreer. It changed the way I looked at things in a big way. Highly recommend.
I know I am old because the one clue I had to google was the Taylor Swift song.
This made my day! Fun way to start off the new month!
Very relaxing. Never solved a Sunday so quickly, 28min.

People seem to be lining up around the BLOCK water cooler this morning to discuss how great this puzzle is. And rightly so, in my opinion.

Can’t believe UTTER ROT is in the puzzle today, because just last night my top bed collapsed onto the bottom bed. The wood finally decayed right to the center of the posts holding it up, which broke clean in half. Which is lucky, so that I could rely on that anecdote, because my spooneristic story about the howling and fighting of male river weasels was probably not ready for this morning anyway. But look it up: the otter rut is quite amazing to watch.
Can someone please explain the cluing for STONEWALL?

As as often my experience with complicated tricks in New York Times crossword puzzles I solved this one in a normal amount of time with a normal amount of pleasure without paying much attention to the tricks and contortions enjoyed by the creators.  Whatever lifts their boat is okay with me but seldom do I enjoy such additional complexities.  For me puzzles are simply about language.

Does anyone else feel cheated, as I do?

I was finishing up the puzzle, looking forward to the second puzzle of figuring out the maze (and the book), when, upon entering the last letter of the crossword, the computer solved the maze for me.

I feel like I missed out on half the fun of this puzzle.
Harumph!

Holy smokes, that was fun!!

The Sunday morning solve is my favorite time of the week so my appreciation skyrockets when it's a puzzle of this quality.

I loved the "walls". I appreciated the cluing. The maze, if not as original as they first thought, was brilliant. I loved the single rebus in the southeast corner as the "prize" at the end of the maze. And it was just the right amount of crunch for a Sunday.

And they used "utter rot"! - one of the many British colloquialisms I borrow from time to time.

Be Amazed? Indeed I am! Thanks so much Kevin and Zhou!

Wonder if the constructors would give us a sequel themed to Newbery-winning classic Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH (darkish film version: The Secret of NIMH). Of course, then the rats could break free of the puzzle and solve it themselves.

This was such a delightful puzzle!  Question for others and the NYT :  When doing the crosswords online,  is there any way to keep the puzzle from doing an automatic reveal of a visual theme right after you've completed the grid? In this case, there would have been a lot more fun to be had if I could have discovered in my own how to get around the maze and what the circled letters spelled out. But the puzzle, by default, just gives the visual answer to you immediately.  I was disappointed and saddened by this today, and it's happened with other puzzles as well.

Is there anything that can be done?
So much fun! I must be lazy because I loved having the gimmick light up after making the rebus my last entry. Great Sunday

OK, what is wrong with this puzzle. I solved the grid in about 30 mins but got the "almost" message. I labored over what waw wrong for another 20 minutes until I just gave up and clicked reveal. At that point, I was told that I solved the puzzle in 50 mins! What was the hang up?

Really clever puzzle. Tough one for me, and had to look up a couple of things. No big deal - that's just me. 

Answer history search today was for STONEWALL. Interesting change in the clues. In the Shortz era, it's always been some variation on the meaning of the verb. And... in pre-Shortz puzzles it was that way a couple of times, but mostly clued in reference to the civil war general. 

.....

Wonderfully intricate yet simple puzzle by these great constructors.

Will their next puzzle have lab rats stuck in an escape room?
Anyone else finish with 1A? That was impressive

Wow! What a fun puzzle. A day after Halloween, but  loved all the different puzzly tricks and treats!  What wonderful way of waking up my mind and making me giggle too! So tell me, anyone else just love these constructors? Made my Sunday for sure.
Thank you guys for an amazing solve!
After I got TOLDTALES early on, I knew 1 across ended with T. Thinking of mazes I put in RODENT. Took me quite a while to figure out that was incorrect.

Fun! I kept mouthing to myself "homo vedmy" then trying to spell out "_homo vedmy... cheese?" until I had my aha moment, and identifying the missing W got me back on track all the way to the gold star.

I do love a silly gimmick on a Sunday. Bravo! Great work with an especially goofy-looking grid. Thank you! Difficulty was right in the sweet spot for me, keeping me engaged the whole time. Loved the rebus.
Fun puzzle!!  lol

Struggling to understand how obstacle course fits the clue. How are courses in a meal obstacles? It is clear that obstacle works with the other shaded squares, but the wordplay escapes me. Nice puzzle anyway.
Sunday puzzle was aMAZing today! Thanks, Ms. Zhang and Mr. Curry!

A puzzle within a puzzle within a puzzle within a puzzle and with a rebus to boot!
Halloween is over, so no need to be afraid. Just BE AMAZED, be very amazed... 

Thank you, Zhou, for breaking the golden rule of meditation  in the name of crossword construction. And thank you, Kevin, for running with it. Together you've created a fantastic and memorable puzzle! Bravo!

P.S. I guess the pest running around the house as if she were in a maze was a little impish french girl – LA BRAT!

I like this puzzle overall. Sometimes too much cleverness makes my eyes roll too far up in my head, but this one has a payoff. My observation to the constructors is that the clues and answers with the shaded areas and 1A/122A work a lot better than the circle elements/book title. I can’t find a consistency in what’s drawing our questing beast up and down; I’m guessing any average nose would lead them on a more efficient path.
A 24 minute solve today which I think may be my fastest Sunday completion time ever.   Thank you for the puzzle, Zhou and Kevin!
What a brave LABRAT! Along his journey, he encounters a CAT, a DOG, a SIAMESE and a MAMBA. He could have stayed home and enjoyed the ASIAGO. Fun puzzle, nice graphics.

that was fun and fast! 17 minutes faster than my Sunday average
thanks, as always!
I rarely comment but have to say that was a very satisfying and fun puzzle. 🩷🩷🩷

commentBody:
I adore when setters take real advantage of the physically/visuality of the crossword as an art form. 

For me, this puzzle worked on at least four levels

1)  Logistical; the letters all cross to form coherent words, which any good crossword does without dipping too far into crosswordese, onomatopoeia, or green paint. 

2) Conceptual: theme words like WALL, DIVIDER, etc. provide infrastructure here

3) Spatial; one and only one continuous path was created from beginning to end of the grid

4) Audience engagement; after completion of the word fill, there was yet another interactive element in tracing the maze to reveal the book title!!!

Seriously, how did it *only* take them 31 tries?!?

Props props props and highest praise.
Great puzzle except for the rebus at the end. Yes, I got it, but then shouldn't all of the circled blanks represent rebuses as well? Not a biggie, but a bit annoying.
Solving this puzzle's theme requires amazing skill (or luck)--too confusing for me. I'm a labrat who didn't get out of the maze and is starving for cheese.
This was just delightful!

Excellent puzzle and I hadfun doing it, with one point of confused.  Can someone explain how a "stone wall" would be ammo for a slingshot?  Is that an expression Im just not familiar with?  Seems like a wall would be a bit large for a slingshot.
Amazing puzzle! A little too easy, but a joy to solve.

In case you missed it, there was a new and ingenious method of catching RATs demonstrated on the TV show "Shark Tank" recently. The inventor, named Ian Fleming, lived with his hunter father in Africa. The device uses an ingenious method of tempting RATs to climb a magnetic platform. When the magnet is released, the RAT falls into the bucket and resets the magnet for the next RAT. You can catch multiple RATs!! What you do with the bucketful of RATs is your problem, I guess!! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OF-NLSklKk4
This was my first ever Sunday solve, and I managed it completely unaided! Took me over a year. Naturally, I liked this puzzle a lot.
All time personal best Sunday -- 13m28s

Clever and fun, but I got angry when I got the DOGE clue.  Anything that reminds me of this administration and Musk in particular is nauseating.  Is the constructor CLUE-less about these kinds of trigger words?

Not just one  (the long phrase clues each including a divider synonym), not two (the circled letters spelling out the book title), not three (the final square is a rebus), not  four (the rat and the maze graphic) but five (the title pun) clever gimmick/tricks in one eminently solvable puzzle??? Holy wordplay Batman! Best Sunday puzzle ever. Congratulations to the authors!

Odd puzzle. Not super hard but took ages to finish. 

On my iPhone, when there is one, the hint/ note on these never show up for me until the puzzle is complete. Anyone else?

What a delightful Sunday solve! The clues were not too difficult which made the actual gameplay work-- though the top middle section had me stumped for a while (anyone else's mind go to pulling a PRANK instead of a HAMMY?). This one was loads of fun!
A-mazing puzzle! Of course I would expect nothing less from these two. And now I want cheese.

Clever! Nice visual, too. Many of us working in corporate jobs back in the late 90s will remember being meetings and exercises built around that little book. The people who analyzed themselves as being most open to change were the people who were the least open to change!

A totally fun solve. Layers, which I adore. And a maze! 

In the top left corner, which I did last, I had "ere" instead of AGO and couldn't believe Scrabble stole BINGO's winning shout. (Doesn't the Scrabble dictionary have enough words of its own?) And for some very strange reason, I was thinking MughaL instead of MONGOL. I have no explanation for that other than the severe limitations of my grade school World History course. (Our teacher told us she was going to leave out China--and did.)

But then LABRAT, ASIAGO cheese and the MONGOL Golden Horde announced their entrance all together and I was done. Except for checking everything before filling in the last square. Even the checking was decidedly unboring, another journey through the maze to get the name of the book, which yielded a third verification of that single rebus.

It did not feel as quick as it was. And, lest it be too quick, the constructors gave links to Patrick Merrell puzzles, many of which I have not solved. Oh frabjous day.
Beat my best Sunday solve time for the second week in a row. Finished it in 9:41.
Fun, cute. But too easy for a Sunday. This solved in whursday time. For Sundays, I like to lounge about with the puzzle because I have the time.
The Rebus is not working on the only square it is intended for ( i experimented on several others).  No "solution" suggested has thus far worked.  We'll see if time heals all "words."
Quite a-maze-ing! Fun Sunday puzzle.

Although for 111D I dutifully filled in TEX, I really wanted it to be TEd: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WtbqbQawo-A&list=RDWtbqbQawo-A&start_radio=1 From the "what were they thinking?' files, a more Peaceful Kind of Beethoven: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BXsZfFupGmo&list=RDBXsZfFupGmo&start_radio=1

Fun solve!  And only one rebus, which I found very near then end of the puzzle, appropriately.  

However, I can't tell you how long I had to wonder if "Labrat" was a character in some famous work of fiction that I had somehow missed, a detective, or a victim like Valjean.  Huge head-slap when I finally separated it into two words!

@Anastasia What is meant by “green paint”? Never heard of this before

"Green paint" is shorthand for a multi-word entry, usually in the form of ADJECTIVE NOUN, which has no meaning beyond the literal "a NOUN which is ADJECTIVE"; such entries are usually frowned upon in crossword puzzles. For example, RED FLAG could be clued as [Warning sign], and BLACK FLAG could be clued as ["TV Party" band], but you'd be hard-pressed to find a clue for ORANGE FLAG beyond... um... [Thing that waves in the air and is the color between red and yellow]. The term was invented back in 2004 by Patrick Berry, who in his Crossword Constructor's Handbook calls out GREEN PAINT as an example of the sort of technically-a-thing entry lesser constructors might cobble together in a grid, noting that "it's [hard] to conjure up a hypothetical reference work that would bother to list GREEN PAINT." Ironically, several constructors have put GREEN PAINT in puzzles clued in reference to Berry's terminology, meaning the entry GREEN PAINT is not green paint.
